claim: `curl -X <method>` sets the method word used in the HTTP request (Commands table, Command and Key options cells).
reasoning: The man page on this machine documents `-X, --request <method>` as "Change the method to use when starting the transfer" and, for HTTP, "Specifies a custom request method to use when communicating with the HTTP server. The specified request method is used instead of the method otherwise used (which defaults to GET)." Short and long forms are correctly paired as -X / --request. Verified empirically: `curl -w '%{method}' -X DELETE ...` reported method DELETE.

claim: Common mistake cell: expecting `-X` to change behaviour — it only changes the method word.
reasoning: Man page, verbatim: "This option only changes the actual word used in the HTTP request, it does not alter the way curl behaves."

claim: `-X HEAD` does not make a proper HEAD request; `-I` does (Commands table and Knowledge check 5).
reasoning: Man page, verbatim: "So for example if you want to make a proper HEAD request, using -X HEAD does not suffice. You need to use the -I, --head option." Knowledge check 5 also states the short/long pairing `-I, --head`, which matches the man page's option header exactly.

claim: The method set with `-X` is reused on redirects followed with `-L`.
reasoning: Man page, verbatim: "The method string you set with -X, --request is used for all requests, which if you for example use -L, --location may cause unintended side-effects when curl does not change request method according to the HTTP 30x response codes." The -L entry states the same from the other side: "The method set with -X, --request overrides the method curl would otherwise select to use."

claim: Worked example `curl -X DELETE https://example.com/orders/42` sends an HTTP request with an explicitly chosen method.
reasoning: Run empirically: the request was issued with method DELETE (curl -w '%{method}' reported DELETE) and the origin answered 405, i.e. the method word was genuinely sent and understood by the server. The example is syntactically valid and does what the Purpose cell says.
source: empirical run of curl 8.7.1 against https://example.com/orders/42; man curl -X, --request

claim: `curl -i` shows the response headers, including the status line, along with the body; `-i` is the include-response-headers option.
reasoning: Man page: "-i, --include (HTTP FTP) Include response headers in the output." Verified empirically: `curl -i https://example.com` printed "HTTP/2 200" and the header block ahead of the body.

claim: `-I` fetches the headers only, by issuing a HEAD request.
reasoning: Man page: "-I, --head (HTTP FTP FILE) Fetch the headers only! HTTP-servers feature the command HEAD which this uses to get nothing but the header of a document." Verified empirically: `curl -I https://example.com` returned the status line and headers with no body.

claim: Worked example `curl -i https://example.com` produces the described output (headers plus body).
reasoning: This is the exact example the curl man page itself gives under -i, --include, and running it returned the HTTP/2 200 status line, the header block, and the page body.

claim: Common mistake cell: `-i` adds headers to the normal response while `-I` issues a HEAD request and returns headers only — the two are distinct options.
reasoning: Both options are separately documented with the stated meanings, and the empirical runs differ exactly as described: -i returned headers plus the HTML body, -I returned headers alone. No claim of universality beyond curl itself is made, and both options have been in curl since long before 8.x, so the claim holds across the curl builds a candidate would meet.

claim: Quick reference row carries the marker and its examinability cell is correct: "SELECT is the only one of the five that changes nothing."

The row's own sentence names five things — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and JOIN — and two of them change nothing: SELECT and JOIN.
